dimension: API routes and the service layer
summary: The HTTP request path is in better shape than the background service layer: admin.service.ts and analytics.service.ts are cached, paginated, and column-projected, and lib/auth/middleware.ts does no per-request DB work beyond one cached entitlement check. Almost all the waste sits in cron-driven services. The dominant finding is that lib/services/scheduler.service.ts's email retry is a self-feeding loop: it re-sends failed emails without a retry counter and without marking the source row, and each re-send inserts a brand-new failed row that becomes the next tick's input. Live production shows 44,510 `group_verification_link` email_logs rows generated from 5 real verification requests all-time (none since 2026-08-16), still growing ~1,030/day. The whole email path accounts for 192,208 statements and 22.3 minutes — 6.6% of all database execution time and roughly 31% of all transactions over 120 days — with a 42,944:525 failure-to-success ratio. Secondary themes: a surviving SQL join fan-out in the superadmin analytics endpoint that overstates a real group's loan book 30×, 34,564 no-op reconciliation runs each writing a permanent audit row, and a codebase-wide misconception that `Promise.all` over a single PoolClient runs in parallel (pg serializes per connection — 43 such blocks).

findings.title: retryFailedEmails is a self-feeding amplification loop: 44,510 emails generated from 5 real requests, still growing ~1,030/day
findings.evidence:
lib/services/scheduler.service.ts:72-104. The SELECT at :75 filters only `status='failed'` + a 24h window — there is NO retry counter, contradicting the function's own doc comment at :71 ("fewer than 3 retries"). The loop at :86 calls sendTemplatedEmail, which reaches lib/email/adapters/resend.ts:21 and INSERTs a brand-new email_logs row; the source row is never updated, so it is re-selected every tick AND its retry becomes the next tick's input.
Live prod proof (5 independent queries):
(1) `select template_key,status,count(*),count(distinct "to") from email_logs group by 1,2` → group_verification_link: 40,519 failed + 3,545 queued + 446 sent = 44,510 rows, to exactly 1 distinct recipient.
(2) `select channel,count(*),max(created_at) from registrant_verifications group by 1` → only 5 email-channel rows ALL-TIME, newest 2026-08-16 19:37. `select prosrc ilike '%delete%' from pg_proc where proname='start_registrant_verification'` → false, so the table is not pruned. The only legitimate producer fired 5 times ever, none in 19 days.
(3) `select type,status,count(*),max(updated_at) from job_queue where type='email_weekly_summary'` → 13 completed, 1 failed, LAST RUN 2026-08-31. Yet `select date_trunc('day',created_at)::date,template_key,count(*) from email_logs where created_at>now()-interval '6 days'` shows weekly_summary rows created every single day through 2026-09-04 (74–116/day). The weekly producer has not run in 4 days; only the retry loop can be writing these.
(4) `select left(last_error,300),count(*) from job_queue where type='email_retry_failed'` → 897 × "Timed out in processing; reset by stuck-job sweep"; 4,475 total attempts. Each timed-out pass still committed its 50 inserts before dying.
(5) pg_stat_statements: `UPDATE email_logs SET status=$3, error_message=$1` = 42,944 calls vs `UPDATE ... status='sent'` = 525 calls — a 98.8% provider failure rate feeding the loop.
findings.impact:
Steady-state 1,150 new email_logs rows/day and ~1,150 outbound Resend API calls/day that all fail, from a queue with zero legitimate work. Across the 120-day pg_stat_statements window the email path burns 192,208 statements and 1,340,327 ms (22.3 min) = 6.6% of the database's entire 340-minute exec time, and ~192k of 624,221 total BEGINs (~31% of ALL transactions). email_logs is 47,262 rows / 21 MB. It permanently occupies a job-queue slot (email_retry_failed: 4,493 pending), which is a direct contributor to the queue starvation already tracked in Sentry KITABUYETU-1. Separately, scheduler.service.ts:92 passes `vars: {}`, so even a retry that succeeded would deliver `

{}

` — the loop cannot produce a useful email even in the success case.
findings.recommendation: Three changes, all in lib/services/scheduler.service.ts:72-104. (1) Add a real bound: an `attempts` / `retried_at` column on email_logs, `WHERE attempts < 3`, and UPDATE the source row inside the loop so it cannot be re-selected. (2) Exclude retry-generated sends from the candidate set (e.g. a `reference_type='retry'` marker) so a retry's own failure row is never itself retried. (3) Carry the original `vars` forward (persist them on email_logs or drop the retry feature entirely — it has never delivered a correct email). Before shipping, one-off delete the ~44,000 orphan rows. Given the loop has produced zero successful useful sends in its life, disabling the email_retry_failed job type is a legitimate immediate mitigation.

findings.title: The retry sweep's SELECT * pulls 202,457 wide rows for 5 columns and then does 50 sequential provider calls per pass
findings.evidence:
lib/services/scheduler.service.ts:75-83 — `SELECT * FROM email_logs ... LIMIT 50`. pg_stat_statements: 27,894 calls, 1,028,942 ms total (17.1 min), 202,457 rows returned. This is the SELECT-*-over-email_logs the audit brief asked me to locate.
`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS)` on live prod: `Index Scan using idx_email_logs_group_id ... Rows Removed by Filter: 418 ... width=343 ... Buffers: shared hit=786 ... Execution Time: 15.7 ms` — width 343 bytes/row across all 21 columns (including the `error_message` text column), while the loop body at :86-96 reads only 5: template_key, "to", group_id, reference_id, reference_type. `information_schema.columns` confirms 21 columns on email_logs.
The consumption loop at :86 is a bare sequential `for...await` with a network email send per iteration — 50 provider round trips serialized, which is why 897 runs hit the 6-minute stuck-job threshold (lib/jobs/db.ts:136, resetStuckJobs).
findings.impact: 17.1 minutes of database exec time (5% of the DB's total 340 min) and roughly 55 MB of row data shipped over the wire, for 5 columns' worth of need. The sequential provider calls make the job structurally unable to finish inside a Vercel function budget, so it never marks itself complete — which is exactly what turns a bounded retry into finding #1's unbounded loop.
findings.recommendation: Project the five columns actually used instead of `*` (drops row width ~343→~90 bytes). Add a partial index on `(created_at) WHERE status='failed'` so the filter isn't discarding 418 of 1,178 scanned rows. Replace the sequential `for...await` with a bounded `Promise.all` over chunks (e.g. 5 at a time) so a pass completes inside the function budget, and lower LIMIT 50 to something the budget can actually absorb.

findings.title: SQL join fan-out survives in getPlatformAnalytics — GET /api/admin/analytics reports THE FIONA'S loan book as KES 32.1M instead of KES 1.07M (30x)
findings.evidence:
lib/services/admin.service.ts:1318-1330 (query body 1319-1329), served by app/api/admin/analytics/route.ts:10. `groups` is LEFT JOINed to three independent one-to-many tables — group_members (:1324), contributions (:1325), loans (:1326) — and then SUMs contributions.amount (:1321) and loans.principal_amount (:1322) over the multiplied row set. `COUNT(DISTINCT gm.id)` is protected by DISTINCT; the two SUMs are not. This is the same defect class PR #105 removed from six other service files.
Verified on live production by running the exact query against a correlated-subquery control in one statement:
  THE FIONA'S      — contributions truth 1,550.00 vs fan-out 31,000.00 (20x); loan_book truth 1,070,000.00 vs fan-out 32,100,000.00 (30x)
  CAPITAL POINT    — contributions truth 1,780.00 vs fan-out 16,020.00 (9x)
  Joka Ezra        — contributions truth 310.00 vs fan-out 2,170.00 (7x)
Control (falsification): the same statement returned equality for the other 6 of 9 groups (those with no contributions or no loans), so the query CAN agree — the three mismatches are real, not an artifact of my comparison.
findings.impact: The superadmin analytics dashboard displays a KES 32.1M loan book for a group that has lent KES 1.07M — a 31-million-shilling overstatement on the platform's own reporting surface, cached for 120s and refreshed indefinitely. `ORDER BY contributions DESC LIMIT 10` at :1328-1329 ranks by the inflated number, so "top groups" is ordered on corrupt data too. Cost is correctness rather than CPU (the tables are small), but it is the last known instance of a bug class the team already paid to fix once.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite as three LATERAL subqueries, matching the pattern PR #105 established elsewhere: `FROM public.groups g LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT count(*) ... FROM group_members ...) gm ON true LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT sum(amount) ... FROM contributions ...) c ON true LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT sum(principal_amount) ... FROM loans ...) l ON true`. Then add a regression test asserting the endpoint's loan_book equals the correlated-subquery value, since this class has now recurred after being fixed.

findings.title: 98.4% of M-Pesa reconciliation runs find nothing yet each writes an audit row and two transactions — 34,564 junk rows
findings.evidence:
lib/services/mpesa-reconciliation.service.ts:115-121 INSERTs a `mpesa_reconciliations` row with status='running' BEFORE any check for work; the scan only happens afterwards at :128-142, and :323-331 UPDATEs the same row to 'completed' unconditionally.
Live prod: `select reconciliation_type,status,count(*), count(*) filter (where coalesce(transactions_checked,0)=0 and coalesce(mismatches_found,0)=0 and coalesce(resolved_count,0)=0) from mpesa_reconciliations group by 1,2` → stk/completed: 35,141 runs of which **34,564 (98.4%) recorded 0 checked, 0 mismatches, 0 resolved**.
Corroborating pg_stat_statements: the scan `SELECT id, checkout_request_id FROM mpesa_stk_requests WHERE status=$2 AND initiated_at<$1 LIMIT $3` ran 35,137 times and returned 577 rows TOTAL (0.016 rows/call).
findings.impact: ~70,300 write transactions (INSERT + UPDATE) plus 35,137 scan statements over 120 days, producing 35,141 permanently-retained rows (4.3 MB) that carry no information — against a platform with 49 payments in total. Every one of those writes is a separate pool connection acquisition (see the connection-churn finding), and every one occupies a job-queue turn in a queue that is already starving.
findings.recommendation: Invert the order in runReconciliation: run the `stale` scan first and return early when it is empty, opening the mpesa_reconciliations row only when there is work. Add a retention sweep for existing no-op rows (`DELETE FROM mpesa_reconciliations WHERE transactions_checked=0 AND mismatches_found=0 AND resolved_count=0 AND created_at < now() - interval '7 days'`). Optionally back off the mpesa_reconcile schedule from every-5-minutes given 577 stale STK rows in four months.

findings.title: 43 Promise.all blocks issue queries on a single PoolClient, which node-postgres serializes — the parallelism is cosmetic
findings.evidence:
Verified against the installed driver, not assumed: node_modules/pg/lib/client.js:579-599 — `_pulseQueryQueue()` only dispatches when `this.readyForQuery === true`, sets it false while a query is active, and otherwise leaves the query on `_queryQueue`. pg 8.20.0. A PoolClient wraps exactly one connection, so N concurrent `client.query()` calls execute strictly one at a time.
A scan of app/api + lib found 43 `Promise.all([...])` blocks whose members are all `client.query`/`db.query` on the same client. Worst offenders by query count: lib/services/admin.service.ts:200 (7 queries — getPlatformStats, read and confirmed in source), lib/services/admin.service.ts:379 (6), lib/services/sms-analytics.service.ts:65 (6), lib/services/analytics.service.ts:141 (5), lib/services/admin.service.ts:295 (4), lib/services/admin.service.ts:1306 (4), lib/services/shares.service.ts:595 (4).
The worst compound case is lib/services/credit-scores.service.ts:367-388: computeComponents wraps 8 component functions in Promise.all on one client (9 queries once componentLoanRepayment's own inner Promise.all at :451 is counted), and recomputeAll at :151 calls it once per member inside a single transaction — so a 37-member group is ~370 strictly-sequential round trips with the transaction held open throughout.
findings.impact: Every one of these endpoints pays the sum of its query latencies instead of the max. For getPlatformStats that is 7 sequential Vercel→Supavisor round trips where 1 is achievable; for credit-score recompute it is N_members × 9. The DB-side exec time is small (these are tiny tables), so the cost is request latency and function wall-clock — i.e. Vercel compute billing — not database CPU. The pattern is also actively misleading: it reads as optimized code, so nobody revisits it.
findings.recommendation: Two options. Cheap and local: collapse each block into ONE query using scalar subqueries or CTEs (`SELECT (SELECT ...) AS groups, (SELECT ...) AS members, ...`), which is a strict improvement and removes the round trips entirely — ideal for admin.service.ts:200/295/379 where every member is an independent aggregate. Structural: for genuinely independent work, hand each branch its own connection via `Promise.all([withAdminDb(...), withAdminDb(...)])` — but note DB_POOL_MAX defaults to 3 (lib/env.ts:22), so more than three concurrent branches just queue (lib/services/report-email.service.ts:94 already requests 4). For credit-scores, rewrite computeComponents as one set-based query over all members rather than per-member.

findings.title: Every email send makes 4 separate uncached transactions, two of which query permanently-empty tables 24,000 times for 0 rows
findings.evidence:
One `sendTemplatedEmail` opens four independent `withAdminDb` transactions — each its own connection acquisition, BEGIN and COMMIT: lib/email/templates/engine.ts:30-41 (loadDbTemplate), lib/email/templates/engine.ts:65-75 (loadBranding), lib/email/adapters/resend.ts:21 (INSERT queued log), lib/email/adapters/resend.ts:65 or :78 (UPDATE final status).
pg_stat_statements, 120-day window:
  `SELECT subject, body FROM email_templates WHERE template_key=$1 ...` — 23,977 calls, **rows returned: 0**
  `SELECT sender_name, logo_url, primary_color, footer_text FROM group_email_branding WHERE group_id=$1` — 23,958 calls, **rows returned: 0**
  `SELECT * FROM email_schedules WHERE is_active=$1 AND next_run_at<=NOW() ...` (lib/services/scheduler.service.ts:9) — 25,601 calls, **rows returned: 0**
Falsification control: `rows` is genuinely populated in this view for other entries (202,457 for the retry SELECT, 47,309 for the email_logs INSERT), so 0 is a real zero and not an unpopulated column. Confirmed against the data: `select count(*) from email_templates` = 0, `select count(*) from group_email_branding` = 0.
findings.impact: ~73,500 statements — each a full connection-acquire/BEGIN/COMMIT cycle — asking three permanently-empty tables the same question, forever. Results are trivially cacheable: template and branding rows change only when someone edits them, and the app already has a `cached()` Redis helper (lib/redis/index.ts:196) that admin.service.ts uses. Because these are 2 of the 4 transactions per email, halving them roughly halves the email path's connection-acquisition rate.
findings.recommendation: Wrap loadDbTemplate and loadBranding in `cached()` with a 5-minute TTL keyed on (templateKey, groupId, locale) and groupId, invalidated on template/branding writes; a negative result is worth caching too since DEFAULT_TEMPLATES already provides the fallback. Merge resend.ts's queued-INSERT and status-UPDATE into a single INSERT after the provider returns (the pre-insert exists to survive a crash mid-send, but 3,837 rows are permanently stranded at 'queued' today, so it is not achieving that anyway). Guard processDueSchedules with a cheap `EXISTS` probe, or stop scheduling it while email_schedules is empty.

findings.title: Near-zero connection reuse: 527,415 pooler authentications against 624,221 transactions (0.85 new connections per transaction)
findings.evidence:
pg_stat_statements: `SELECT * FROM pgbouncer.get_auth($1)` — 527,415 calls, 288,137 ms. Supavisor runs this once per incoming client connection, so the count is the app's connection count. Against `begin` = 624,221 calls and `commit` = 605,405 calls, that is 0.845 new pooler connections per transaction.
Control showing the pooler itself is not the churn source: `pg_stat_activity` currently holds exactly ONE `postgres`/`Supavisor` backend, and `pg_stat_database.sessions` = 321,646 — Supavisor multiplexes onto a stable backend pool, so the 527k figure is client→pooler connects originating in the app, not backend churn.
Mechanism in code: lib/db/index.ts:64-74 builds the pool with `idleTimeoutMillis: 10_000` and `max: env.DB_POOL_MAX` (default 3, lib/env.ts:22). On Vercel the instance is frozen after each response; the 10s idle timer fires on thaw and reaps every idle client, so an instance reused after >10s (every 5-minute cron tick) reconnects from zero. Compounding it, every `withAdminDb`/`withDb` call takes a fresh `pool.connect()`, and the codebase calls them per-statement rather than per-request — 4 per email (see previous finding), 2 per reconciliation run, 1 per CSV row in some paths.
findings.impact: 527,415 TCP + TLS + SCRAM handshakes from Lambda in 120 days. 288 seconds of that is measurable database CPU for get_auth alone; the client-side handshake cost (typically 30-80 ms each from a serverless function) is not visible in pg_stat_statements but is billed as Vercel function wall-clock — order of hours over the window. Every finding above that says "one transaction per row" is also a finding about this number.
findings.recommendation: Raise `idleTimeoutMillis` from 10s to 60s or more (Supavisor session mode with max 3 per instance makes holding a connection cheap, and the pooler, not Postgres, absorbs the concurrency). Then attack the call-site multiplier: batch the per-statement `withAdminDb` calls identified in the email, reconciliation and write-loop findings so one logical operation takes one connection instead of N. Measure after: the get_auth:begin ratio is a good ongoing health metric and should fall well below 0.1.

findings.title: Bulk member import runs 3-4 sequential queries per CSV row — up to 5,000 rows in one HTTP request inside one transaction
findings.evidence:
lib/services/import.service.ts:297-388, on the request path via the import commit endpoint. Per row inside the loop: `client.query` at :301 (duplicate-in-group check joining group_members to members on phone), :317 (existing member lookup), :325 (update), :346 (insert new member). `MAX_ROWS` at :21 defaults to 5,000 and is enforced at :120/:548/:625/:891. The whole loop runs inside a single `withTransaction`.
The same file already knows the fix: line 131, in the PREVIEW path, reads `// Counties cached once per import to avoid N queries.` — the commit path never got the same treatment.
findings.impact: A 5,000-row import issues 15,000-20,000 strictly sequential round trips in one request, holding one transaction open the entire time. At even 2 ms per round trip that is 30-40 s; at a realistic serverless-to-pooler 10 ms it is 150-200 s, which exceeds most Vercel function budgets — and because it is one transaction, a timeout rolls back every row already imported, so a large import can never succeed and can never partially succeed either. Currently latent (9 groups, 37 members), but it is the code path a new customer onboarding hits first.
findings.recommendation: Hoist the duplicate check out of the loop: one query fetching all existing (phone → member_id, membership_id) pairs for the group, held in a Map, replaces the per-row queries at :301 and :317. Batch the inserts at :346 into multi-row `INSERT ... VALUES (...),(...) ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id` in chunks of 500. That takes a 5,000-row import from ~20,000 round trips to roughly 12. Separately, move commit off the request path into the job queue for anything above a few hundred rows.

findings.title: Cron fan-out services walk groups and members one at a time with a network send per item and no batching or resumability
findings.evidence:
lib/services/report-email.service.ts:84-155 (sendWeeklySummaries): one query for all active groups, then PER GROUP five separate `withAdminDb` transactions — four aggregates in a Promise.all at :94 plus an officers lookup at :138 — then a sequential send per officer at :149. The Promise.all at :94 requests 4 concurrent pool connections against DB_POOL_MAX=3 (lib/env.ts:22), so the fourth always queues.
lib/services/statement-email.service.ts:113-140 (sendAllGroupMemberStatements): a sequential per-group loop at :121 wrapping a sequential per-member email send at :83 — a nested fan-out with a provider call at the leaf, no concurrency, no cursor, no cap.
Same shape at lib/services/governance.service.ts:406-410 and lib/services/mpesa-reports.service.ts:29-39/:99.
pg_stat_statements corroborates the per-group multiplication: the two per-group aggregates `SELECT COALESCE(SUM(principal_amount),$2) ... FROM loans WHERE group_id=$1` and `SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM group_members WHERE group_id=$1 AND joined_at >= ...` each ran 165 times, i.e. once per group per run, where one GROUP BY over all groups would have run once.
findings.impact: Each job's cost is O(groups × members) sequential network calls with no checkpoint, so it grows linearly with customers and is guaranteed to exceed the function budget well before the platform is large. When it does, resetStuckJobs (lib/jobs/db.ts:136) marks it timed out and re-runs it from the beginning — re-sending every email it already sent, with no idempotency key. That is the identical failure shape as the retry loop in finding #1 and is why account_statement shows 64 failed / 24 stranded-queued rows and weekly_summary 2,110 failed rows for 4 distinct recipients.
findings.recommendation: Replace the per-group aggregate queries with a single `GROUP BY group_id` query returning every group's numbers in one round trip (7 groups × 5 transactions → 2). For the fan-out itself, enqueue one job per group (or per batch of members) rather than one job for the whole platform, so a timeout loses one group's work instead of all of it and the queue's own retry/backoff applies at the right granularity. Add a per-recipient idempotency key so a re-run cannot re-send.

findings.title: sweepPaybillTransactions has no scheduler at all — it has executed exactly once in the platform's lifetime
findings.evidence:
`grep -rn 'runReconciliation|sweepPaybillTransactions'` across lib and app: sweepPaybillTransactions (lib/services/mpesa-reconciliation.service.ts:223) is reachable ONLY from app/api/v1/mpesa/reconcile/route.ts:41/:55 — a manual, authenticated endpoint. There is no job-queue wiring; lib/jobs/handlers.ts:250 wires the scheduled `mpesa_reconcile` job to runReconciliation only.
Live prod: `select reconciliation_type,count(*),min(created_at),max(created_at) from mpesa_reconciliations group by 1` → paybill_sweep: **1 row, 2026-07-29 18:23:57, that is both the oldest and the newest**. Against stk: 35,141 runs, newest 2026-09-04 13:10.
findings.impact: Inverted priority in the reconciliation subsystem: the sweep that does nothing 98.4% of the time runs every five minutes, while the sweep that actually detects completed C2B transactions with no domain record — the exact class of failure behind the already-diagnosed missing paybill receipt UI3QZ4ZNVQ — has never been scheduled and has run once, six weeks ago. This is not the job-queue starvation already documented for mpesa_reconcile; it is a complete absence of wiring, so no amount of queue-throughput work will ever make it run.
findings.recommendation: Add a `mpesa_paybill_sweep` job type wired to sweepPaybillTransactions on an hourly schedule (its own doc comment at :220-221 already establishes it is fully idempotent via the UNIQUE mpesa_unrouted.receipt, so re-running is safe). At the same time, demote runReconciliation's cadence — 577 stale STK rows in four months does not justify every five minutes.

findings.title: Write loops that open one full transaction per row instead of one multi-row statement
findings.evidence:
Four sites, each `await withAdminDb(...)` (or the equivalent) inside a loop, so every iteration is a separate pool acquisition + BEGIN + statement + COMMIT:
- app/api/v1/email/preferences/route.ts:46 — PUT loops the submitted preferences, one transaction each, plus a `.catch()` fallback at :60 that opens a SECOND transaction on conflict (worst case 2N).
- lib/services/campaign.service.ts:104 — one transaction per campaign recipient, uncapped by the group's member count.
- app/api/v1/mpesa/bill-manager/route.ts:156 — up to 100 sequential INSERTs (better: they share one outer withAdminDb, so it is N round trips rather than N transactions).
- lib/services/accounting.service.ts:239 — seedDefaultAccountsInTx issues 20 sequential INSERTs (DEFAULT_ACCOUNTS has 20 entries) on the group-registration path.
findings.impact: Small in absolute terms today given real volumes (9 groups, 37 members), but these are the multipliers behind the connection-churn ratio and they scale linearly with customer size. The email/preferences case is the only one on an interactive request path; a member saving preferences pays ~8-16 sequential transactions for what is one logical save.
findings.recommendation: Collapse each into a single multi-row `INSERT ... VALUES (...),(...),... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` in one transaction. For email/preferences that also removes the try/catch-into-a-second-transaction fallback at :60, which is masking a real ON CONFLICT target problem rather than handling one.

findings.title: Tenant reads cost 6 round trips for 1 statement: setTenantLocals issues three separate set_config calls
findings.evidence:
lib/db/index.ts:121-131 — setTenantLocals runs `SELECT set_config($1,$2,TRUE)` three times sequentially (four when organizationId is present, :128-130). lib/db/index.ts:192-202's `query(ctx, sql)` helper wraps ONE caller statement in withDb, so the wire sequence is BEGIN, set_config, set_config, set_config, the actual query, COMMIT = 6 round trips for 1 statement.
pg_stat_statements confirms the shape and the volume: `SELECT set_config($1, $2, $3)` 6,591 calls + `SELECT set_config($1,$2,$3)` 6,409 calls = 13,000, i.e. ~4,300 tenant transactions in 120 days (real user traffic is genuinely tiny, which is why the absolute cost is low).
findings.impact: Two avoidable round trips on every authenticated tenant API call. At a serverless-to-pooler RTT of 10-30 ms that is 20-60 ms of pure latency added to every request in the product — user-visible, and it scales with request count rather than data size, so it gets worse as the platform grows while the DB-side cost stays near zero.
findings.recommendation: Collapse the three (or four) calls into a single statement: `SELECT set_config($1,$2,TRUE), set_config($3,$4,TRUE), set_config($5,$6,TRUE)` — still fully parameterised, still transaction-local, one round trip. That takes a single-statement tenant read from 6 round trips to 4. Note this is safe only inside the existing BEGIN; do not attempt to fold BEGIN in with it.

findings.title: The subscription gate's allow-list-only cache means an unentitled group re-queries the database on every single request
findings.evidence:
lib/auth/subscription-gate.ts:233-234 — `const products = await loadActiveProducts(auth.groupId); if (products.size > 0) remember(...)`. A group with zero active subscriptions is never cached, so every request runs loadActiveProducts (:177-186), a full withAdminDb transaction. assertSubscriptionActive (:217) is called from withAuth (lib/auth/middleware.ts:67), i.e. on every tenant route.
Live prod: `select g.name, coalesce(string_agg(distinct s.product||':'||s.status,', '),'(none)') from groups g left join subscriptions s on s.group_id=g.id group by 1` → `coinbankcrypto` has NO subscription rows at all; two more groups hold only `kitabu_yetu:expired`. The other six hold an active subscription and are correctly served from the in-process Map.
findings.impact: Currently bounded — 3 of 9 groups, and two of those are deactivated — so this is a latency issue for a small set rather than a live cost problem today. It matters because it is the failure mode that grows: the moment a cohort of subscriptions lapses (which has happened on this platform before), every request from every lapsed group becomes an uncached database transaction on the hottest code path in the app.
findings.recommendation: Add a short NEGATIVE cache — 5-10 seconds, deliberately far below the 60s positive TTL. That preserves the file's load-bearing correctness rule (documented at :186-200: a group that just paid must not sit behind a stale deny) while capping the worst case at ~6-12 queries per minute per lapsed group instead of one per request. Do not simply cache the empty set at CACHE_TTL_MS; the doc comment explains precisely why that reintroduces "I paid and it's still broken".
